en: Freezing ruins it. The potato goes mealy and the egg weeps water on thawing. There is no good way round this.

A warm stack straight from the tortillería is a moist cooked starch and it moulds fast in a closed bag. Keep it wrapped in a cloth inside a tortillero for the day you buy it; by day two it is stiff and better toasted than eaten soft. Never leave a warm stack sealed in plastic on the counter.

Bag them airtight once cool, at 40 °F (4 °C) or below. They come out of the fridge brittle and crack when folded — steam them for a few seconds or hit them on a dry comal and they come back. Blue-green or white fuzz means the whole stack goes.
Interleave with baking paper so you can pull off two at a time, then double-bag. Thaw in the bag; reheat straight from frozen on a comal.

A published study of black truffle preservation describes the fresh product as having a 'very limited shelf life (maximum of 5–7 days, room temperature)'. In practice nobody should be keeping a truffle on the counter — it loses aroma and water by the hour — but that is the outer bound if you do.

In a sealed glass jar in the coldest part of the fridge, wrapped in kitchen paper that you change every single day. The paper absorbs the water the truffle sweats out; leave the same damp paper on it and you have made a mould incubator. Brush the soil off with a dry brush and do not wash it until the moment you use it. The rice trick is a myth worth killing: rice is a desiccant, it strips the truffle of both moisture and aroma, and all you get in return is faintly scented rice.

Freezing is a real option for black truffles and a poor one for white. Freeze it whole and hard, wrapped tight, and grate it from frozen straight onto the dish — never thaw it, because thawing collapses it into a grey wet lump. Expect to lose a good part of the aroma.

Sealed, upright, in a dark cupboard away from the hob. Almost all commercial truffle oil is an ordinary oil carrying a synthesised aroma compound — 2,4-dithiapentane, the molecule responsible for most of what people recognise as truffle — rather than any truffle, and it keeps exactly as the base oil does. Heat, light and air are what age it.

The aroma goes long before the oil does. Once opened, the volatile compound escapes every time you take the cap off, and a bottle a year old often smells of nothing but oil. Buy small bottles and use them fast. Rancidity — a stale crayon smell — is the separate, later failure.

Slows oxidation. Olive-based oils go cloudy and semi-solid in the fridge and clear again at room temperature, which is harmless. Refrigeration is worth it in a hot kitchen and pointless in a cool one.

This figure is for a genuinely fermented, properly salted pickle — a nukazuke bed, a salt-crock 古漬け — kept cold. NCHFP gives fully fermented pickles about 4 to 6 months in their original container, refrigerated, provided surface scum and moulds are removed regularly, and gives fully fermented sauerkraut 'several months' tightly covered. 浅漬け (asazuke) is the opposite case and the one people get wrong: lightly salted vegetables with no real fermentation and no acid to speak of, made in hours rather than weeks. NCHFP's own quick pickle, the refrigerator dill, ferments for only about a week. Treat asazuke as a salad — cold, covered, a few days at most.
Opened commercial packs and jars. Keep the vegetables under their liquid, sealed, at 4 °C or below.
Not a pantry food once opened, however firm it feels. Unopened retort or vacuum packs follow their own printed date.

Loose or freshly sliced rice cake is a wet rice product: Taiwan’s 農業部 says wet rice foods such as 粄條, 米苔目 and 蘿蔔糕 must be held at 7 °C or below, and TFDA caps refrigerated storage of cooked starchy food at about two days.
Freeze in single portions. Drop the pieces straight into boiling water or sauce from frozen; thawing on the counter makes them gummy outside and hard in the middle.
Unopened.

Unopened, cool, dark and dry. Turrón is mostly almonds and honey, and what ends it is the almond oil going rancid — a stale, painty, cardboard taste — not anything growing. Heat and light accelerate that, so a cupboard, not a windowsill. Turrón blando (Jijona) is a ground almond paste and turns oily faster than the hard Alicante slab.

Once the block is opened, wrap it tightly — turrón duro pulls moisture from the air and goes from brittle to chewy, and turrón blando dries and crumbles. Keep the original foil or press film onto the cut face.

Refrigerating an opened block slows the almond oil going rancid, which is the real limit on how long it lasts. Wrap it airtight first or it will pick up fridge smells and condensation. Let it come back to room temperature before eating; cold turrón is flavourless and dangerously hard on teeth.

Traditional 白干梅 — plums salted at about 20 percent, weighted for a month and then sun-dried — is a preserve, and 農林水産省 says plainly that it is the action of the salt that makes long keeping possible. A jar of the traditional kind lives in a cool dark cupboard and gets better rather than worse. The instruction to keep the salt at 20 percent is not decorative: 農林水産省 warns that reducing it can make the batch fail.

For the modern 調味梅干 sold today — plums desalted and re-seasoned with honey, dashi or shiso, often down at 5 to 8 percent salt. These are refrigerated products with a printed date, not preserves, and once the pack is opened the date no longer applies. Keep them in their liquid, sealed, at 4 °C or below.
Japan's MAFF: store dried goods away from heat, direct sunlight and damp, and reseal the bag tightly. Wakame is very hygroscopic and turns limp and fishy once it takes up moisture.
Sealed. Rehydrated wakame is a fresh food: refrigerate and use within 1 to 2 days.

Leave the green husks on — they are what keeps the white stem from drying — and bag it in the crisper. Black specks in the flesh are the smut fungus that creates the vegetable, not spoilage, though very black stems are past their best.
Keep the dark skins on and the corms slightly damp in a bag; peeled water chestnuts must be covered in water and used within 2 to 3 days.
Water will store indefinitely, though the taste may be impacted by storage conditions, including sunlight, items stored around it and the containers being used to store it.

UH-CTAHR's optimum is 10 to 12 days at 12–14 °C with 90–95 % RH, and it warns that ung choi is injured below 10–14 °C — leaves and stems darken after about 4 days at 1 °C. In a 4 °C home fridge expect 3 to 5 days. Bag it to stop water loss and do not put it on ice.
The skin is thin and loses water quickly, so the fruit shrivels rather than rots. Do not wash before storing; wipe with a dry cloth.
Taiwan's food education platform advises wrapping wax apples in paper before refrigerating, because the bare fruit suffers cold damage. Wash only when you are ready to eat.
NCHFP gives dried vegetables about 6 months at 60 °F and 3 months at 80 °F; Ohio State gives a year at 70 °F. Keep it in a sealed jar — the brittle fans crumble and then absorb damp.

Hong Kong CFS: soaking at room temperature should take no more than two hours, otherwise refrigerate the soaking bowl; use soaked fungus as soon as possible and discard it if it turns slimy or smells abnormal.
CTAHR calls it highly perishable and soft-skinned; each fruit needs padding or it bruises.
CTAHR says to chill it in the field or as soon as possible after harvest.
The frilled edges brown and dry first. Bag the pods and use them while the wings are still crisp.

Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture puts winter melon in the 13–15 °C group along with bananas, sweet potato, ginger and pumpkin — it should not go in a cold fridge whole. A cool, dry, airy corner is right; the waxy bloom on the skin is what preserves it, so do not scrub it off.
Only for a cut piece, which is how it is usually sold: scrape out the seeds and pulp, wrap the cut face in cling film and refrigerate.

A stack of wonton wrappers is fresh wheat dough dusted with starch — treat it exactly like fresh pasta. Keep it sealed and flat at the back of the fridge; the outer sheets dry out and crack within hours of the pack being opened.
Freeze in the original sleeve inside a bag. Thaw the whole block in the fridge overnight — peeling frozen sheets apart tears them.
NCHFP gives dried vegetables about 6 months at 60 °F and 3 months at 80 °F; Ohio State gives dried vegetables a year at 70 °F. Airtight, dark, dry.

This is the one that matters: Hong Kong's Centre for Food Safety says soaking should take no more than two hours at room temperature, and that black fungus must be kept in the refrigerator if it needs to soak overnight. Improperly soaked and stored black fungus can develop bongkrekic acid, which cooking does not destroy. Use soaked fungus at once and throw it out if it turns slimy or smells wrong.

Keep it cold and dry in a paper-lined box. Hong Kong CFS warns that black fungus left soaking or standing warm can develop bongkrekic acid, which cooking will not destroy — discard any that has gone slimy or smells sour.

Refrigeration ensures that commercial sauces and condiments stay fresh for a longer period of time. Shelf-stable commercial worcestershire sauce is safe when stored at room temperature after opening. Quality, not safety, is the reason the labels on these products suggest that they be refrigerated after opening.

Unopened commercial jars keep on the shelf to the printed date. Once opened, commercial XO sauce goes in the fridge — it is mostly dried scallop, dried shrimp and cured ham held under oil, and the oil is what keeps air off it.
Keep the solids submerged under the oil layer and use a clean dry spoon. Top up with a little neutral oil if the surface is exposed.

Homemade XO sauce is a different proposition: fresh garlic, shallot and chilli suspended in oil is exactly the low-acid-produce-under-oil situation that NCHFP warns about. NCHFP's rule for garlic in oil is refrigeration at 4 °C (40 °F) or lower for no more than 4 days, or the freezer for longer. Frying the aromatics until they are genuinely dry and crisp reduces but does not eliminate the risk.
Homemade XO sauce freezes well in a small jar or an ice-cube tray. NCHFP says garlic in oil 'may be frozen for long term storage for up to several months'.
Store in cool, dry place. Must be refrigerated or frozen once opened.

Sealed, cool, dark and dry — a cupboard, not the counter beside the kettle. Good yerba is aged for months or years before sale, so it is a stable dried leaf; what ruins it is damp and light. Keep the bag clipped or decant it into a tin.

Once opened it loses aroma steadily and the dust settles out. Buy the size you will drink. Yerba that smells of hay and nothing else, or of the cupboard, is stale rather than unsafe. A gourd is a different matter entirely: a wet calabash left with damp yerba in it grows mould within a day, so empty and dry it after every session.
Do not freeze it. Yerba is hygroscopic and a freezer means condensation every time you open the bag, which is the one thing that genuinely spoils it.
Store fresh yuzu wrapped in plastic in your refrigerator.
For long term storage of leftovers, freeze the juice and zest.

Airtight jar, dry cupboard, out of sunlight and away from the heat of the stove. Za'atar is not a pure spice blend — the toasted sesame in it carries oil, and rancid sesame is what usually spoils an old jar, tasting flat and slightly bitter before it smells of anything. Buy small quantities; the dried thyme and the sumac both fade visibly, and a brown, dusty-looking za'atar has nothing left.
Sensible for a large tub, because it is the sesame oil you are protecting. Seal it well and let it warm before opening so it does not take up condensation.

Sealed vacuum sachets and tins keep to the printed date in a cool dry cupboard. Taiwan's 農業部 describes 榨菜 as mustard stem nodules field-dried, shade-dried for a day or two, then salted, turned twice during fermentation and aged for 4 to 6 months — it is a salt preserve, which is why the unopened pack does not need cold.

Once the sachet is cut, get the contents into a sealed jar in the fridge. Shredded, seasoned 榨菜絲 in oil is the most perishable form — it is wet, it has been rinsed of some of its salt, and it moulds at the surface within weeks. A whole knob keeps better than shreds. Rinse only what you are about to cook.
Hanging a bundle of zongzi in the kitchen is the traditional habit and the dangerous one. Get them into the fridge or freezer as soon as they stop steaming.

Glutinous rice packed around fatty pork and egg yolk is a textbook Bacillus cereus food. TFDA caps refrigerated storage of cooked starchy food at about two days at 5 °C or below; beyond that it must go in the freezer.

TFDA says to move uneaten zongzi into the freezer at -18 °C or below as quickly as possible, but also warns against leaving them there too long if you want the original flavour. Thaw in the fridge, then steam or microwave until the centre is genuinely hot — a zongzi reheated only on the outside is the classic post-Dragon-Boat-Festival poisoning.
